Docs

The rules in full

Rule 17 / 2026-11-25. The same text for every company. There is no setting per company.

Free to use. The rules, every version and this page are published under CC BY 4.0; using them costs nothing. The priced receipt is an optional proof of conformity, not part of the rules. The licence, and what the receipt is.

This page, with the list at What else decides whether STK signs, is everything that decides whether STK signs. Nothing else does. The list of actions, each on one line: The rules; each action in detail on its own page, linked from there.

Rule 17 / 2026-11-25 is the name of this version: its number and the day it was published. Below the name, the text is fixed by its SHA-256: Rule 17 · 29ac953f826078fd15f332c706b846a447162d2f80aee3e10dc798ea97a6af1a. GET https://api.stk-evidence.com/v1/rules gives the same text, its number, its hash, its date and STK's signature of them, no key. Every receipt names the Rule it was signed under.

STK permission rules

These rules are the same for every company. STK answers from these rules and from nothing else: not the
words of the conversation (STK never receives them), not a confidence number.

Each intent is one act. read: answer what is, and change nothing. change: change something. decide: make a
decision. A conversation goes to a person for two reasons only: a law names a person for its act, or a trigger
happened. An intent is on the Never list only when a law names a person for that act; the law, its section and
the address of its official text, as STK reads them, are written beside it below. Every other intent is on the
Permitted list. When no jurisdiction is given, the strictest is followed: an intent on the Never list goes to a
person when a law beside it applies on the day, in any jurisdiction. The answer is the same whatever jurisdictions
are given: they are kept in the row and change no answer (the Checked list below is empty, and a jurisdiction not
on it is answered as if none were given). This is the line read on 2026-11-25; it holds in every jurisdiction read
that day. This line does not change.

The Checked list places no intent.
A jurisdiction not on the Checked list for the subject of an intent is answered as if none were given.
What was read of each jurisdiction's laws until 2026-11-25 is kept, as it was read, at the end of these rules. No
answer depends on it.

Every intent below is of the domain conversation: an act of an AI in a conversation with a customer. Its full
name is conversation. followed by the name listed (conversation.claim.status); either form is read as the same.

1. trigger is not unknown: escalate. Pass unknown only when none of the Triggers below happened in the
   conversation; when one did, pass its name.
2. intent is other: escalate. other is a conversation that could not be told as any act, so it is not known what
   it would do.
3. intent is on the Never list and a law beside it applies on the day: escalate; when jurisdictions are given,
   only if such a law is one of theirs.
4. intent is on no list (a name these rules do not have): escalate.
5. intent is on the Closed list: escalate.
6. Otherwise: finish.

Triggers (6), each one passed when it happened at any point in the conversation, whatever the intent:
- customer_asked: the customer asked for a person (a human, an agent, a representative, a supervisor, a manager), or said they do not want to deal with the AI, in any words, once.
- distressed: the customer said they are frightened, panicking, crying or cannot cope, or spoke of a medical emergency, of harming themselves, or of a danger to someone's life now.
- angry: the customer insulted or swore at the company, its staff or the AI, or said they are angry or furious.
- bereavement: the customer said that someone has died, or the conversation is about the account, the plan or the affairs of someone who has died.
- threat: the customer threatened harm to anyone or to property, or said someone is threatening or forcing them.
- legal_claim: the customer spoke of a lawyer, a lawsuit, a court, a regulator or an ombudsman, a formal complaint or a formal appeal, or of taking legal action.

Never (25): account.refuse, claim.deny_medical, claim.refuse, collections.refuse, coverage.deny_medical, coverage.refuse, credit.refuse, decision.appeal, decision.review, dispute.refuse, fraud.refuse, insclaim.decide, insclaim.partial, insclaim.refuse, liability.decide, limit.lower, payment_arrangement.refuse, policy.cancel, policy.nonrenew, policy.refuse, priorauth.deny_medical, priorauth.refuse, refund.refuse, totalloss.decide, transfer.error_refuse

The law that names a person, for each intent on the Never list:
- account.refuse: GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) Art. 22(1) and (3); UK GDPR Arts. 22A and 22C (in force from 2026-02-05: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, s. 80 and Sch. 6, by SI 2026/82, reg. 2(j), (z8); not for a decision taken before that day, reg. 5); C.R.S. § 6-1-1705(1)(a)(II) (Colorado SB 26-189: on the consumer's request, the deployer provides an opportunity for meaningful human review and reconsideration of the consequential decision, to the extent commercially reasonable; definitions in § 6-1-1701(15); applies to decisions made on or after 2027-01-01; enforcement stayed by the order of 2026-04-27 in X.AI LLC v. Weiser, No. 1:26-cv-01515 (D. Weiser, No. 1:26-cv-01515 (D. Colo.); the attorney general's rules, 4 CCR 904-6, not in effect); 11 CCR § 7221(a), (b)(1)(A) (California, regulations under the CCPA: the business provides the consumer with a method to appeal the decision to a human reviewer who has the authority to overturn the decision; for decisions on financial or lending services, § 7001(ddd)(1); from 2027-01-01; not automated decisionmaking technology where the human involvement of § 7001(e)(1) is present; decisions of a financial institution on consumers' nonpublic personal information may be outside it by the exemption for GLBA data in Cal. Code § 1798.145, not verified); Data Protection Act, 2019 (Kenya) s. 35(1) (in force 2019-11-25: a right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning or significantly affects the person; Jurisdictions. Each is given by its code: ISO 3166-1 for a country (US, GB), ISO 3166-2 for a part of one
(US-WA), EU for the European Union; UK is read as GB. A code takes in the laws of what it is part or member of,
and a country's code the laws of its parts (the lists below): US is the laws of the United States and of each
state; US-WA, of the United States and of Washington; DE, of the EU and of Germany; EU, of the EU. Where several
are given, each is applied and the strictest is followed.

Days. A law applies from the day written beside its jurisdiction below (00:00 UTC), and from the day it is cited
when none is written. Before that day it sends no intent to a person; the intent is answered as if that law were
not beside it.

Three kinds of law put an intent on the Never list, each counted in these rules as a law that names a person for it:
- A, a qualified person: a law names who decides by licence or qualification: a physician, a clinical peer, a medical director, a médico, a praticien conseil, a Vertrauensarzt, a medical practitioner. Most laws of the United States beside health intents; ANS Resolução Normativa nº 424/2017; Code de la sécurité sociale, art. L315-1, L315-2; KVG Art. 57, 58; Private Health Insurance Act 2007 s 75-15; and the licences of insurance adjusters: Tex. Ins. Code § 4101, KRS 304.9-430(1)(a), M.G.L. c. 26, § 8G, 보험업법 제185조, CQLR c. D-9.2, and in India a licensed surveyor above a threshold. Each citation says whom
- B, a right on request: a person may ask for a human review of a decision: UK GDPR Art. 22C; C.R.S. § 6-1-1705(1)(a)(II); 11 CCR § 7221; BDSG § 37(1) Nr. 2
- C, a category of decision: a law requires the first decision to be taken by a person because of what is decided, with no request and no licence: GDPR Art. 22(1) and (4), a prohibition in principle that need not be invoked (CJEU C-634/21, SCHUFA, 2023-12-07), unless Art. 22(2) applies; UK GDPR Art. 22B, for special categories of personal data, unless its conditions are met; the IRDAI Master Circular on Health Insurance Business, para. 17(a), a committee; O.C.G.A. § 33-46-7.1(c) (Georgia SB 444, from 2027-01-01), an AI tool that is not the sole basis of an adverse determination and does not supersede the clinical peer's judgment

Two locks. STK's server does not start with a version of these rules that breaks either:
- Lock 1, the law: an intent is on the Never list only with a law that names a person for it, its section and the
  address of its official text written beside it. An intent with no such law is not on the Never list.
  Whatever jurisdictions are given, an intent goes to a person only with a law of kind A, B or C written beside it
  and applying on the day; a law not found is no law. From the version of 2026-11-25 no intent leaves the Never list
  and no answer becomes less strict: the server does not start with a version that would.
- Lock 2: the Triggers list can only get longer: a new version may add a trigger, never take one off or change its
  words. It goes against STK's revenue: STK is paid for each permission, and a trigger only lowers their number.
So every intent is where it is because of a law or its absence, and anyone can check each one against the
official text and the reasons published with it.

* BR: Lei 13.709/2018 (LGPD) Art. 20: a right to request review of a decision taken solely by automated processing; the words requiring the review to be by a natural person ("por pessoa natural") were removed by veto in Lei 13.853/2019; no person required
* IT: Legge 23 settembre 2025, n. 132, art. 7(5) (in force 2025-10-10): diagnosis and the choice of treatment are the physician's; no action of these rules is a diagnosis or a treatment
* JP: 医師法 17条, 20条: medicine is a physician's, and treatment needs the physician's own examination; no action of these rules is either
* NL: Uitvoeringswet AVG art. 40 (in force 2018-05-25): automated decisions a legal obligation or a public task requires, with a person's intervention as their safeguard; no action of these rules is such a decision
* IE: Data Protection Act 2018 s. 57 (in force 2018-05-25): decisions a law authorises; no action of these rules is such a decision
* LK: Personal Data Protection Act No. 9 of 2022 s. 18: not in operation (no day appointed for Part II); not applied
Conditions the laws read put on completing an intent without human review there:
* the intents beside it in KE: Data Protection Act, 2019 s. 35(2): not where the decision is necessary for entering into or performing a contract with the person, authorised by a law with safeguards, or based on the person's consent; then s. 35(3)-(4)
* the intents beside it in NG: Nigeria Data Protection Act, 2023 s. 37(2): contract, a written law with safeguards, or consent; s. 37(3): human intervention, a view, a contest
* the intents beside it in MU: Data Protection Act 2017 s. 38(2): contract, a law with safeguards, or explicit consent
* the intents beside it in RU: Federal Law No. 152-FZ, Art. 16(2): the person's written consent, or a federal law with safeguards
* the intents beside it in FR: Loi n° 78-17, art. 47: the cases of GDPR Art. 22(2)(a) and (c), the rules of the processing told on request
* the intents beside it in CL: Ley N° 19.628 art. 8° bis, letters a, b and c: contract, prior express consent, a law with safeguards; in every case human intervention and review
* the intents beside it in ZA: POPIA s. 71(2): a contract where the person's request was met or measures protect the person; or a law or code of conduct with measures
* the intents beside it in MA: Loi n° 09-08, art. 11: a contract where the person could present observations, or a decision satisfying the person's requests
* the intents beside it in PE: Ley N° 29733, art. 23: the negotiation, conclusion or performance of a contract, or an evaluation for joining a public entity
* claim.deny_medical, coverage.deny_medical, priorauth.deny_medical in US-TX: Tex. Ins. Code § 4201.156(c): an algorithm for administrative support or fraud detection is not prohibited
* dispute.file, dispute.decide, dispute.refuse, transfer.error_decide, transfer.error_refuse in US: completed without human review only with the reasonable investigation of 12 CFR Part 1005 Supp. I, comment 11(c)(4)-5, and Part 1026 Supp. I, comment 13(f)-3: a design that refuses on a single factor without reviewing the relevant information in the institution's own records may violate them (CFPB v. USAA, 2019-BCFP-0001)
* priorauth.decide in FR: an accord préalable for the benefits listed is given after the medical control service, whose missions are exercised by the praticiens conseils (Code de la sécurité sociale, art. L315-1 VIII, L315-2)
* priorauth.decide in CH: the benefits designated under KVG (SR 832.10) Art. 58(3)(a) need the prior consent of the insurer's Vertrauensarzt
* decision.appeal, coverage.deny_medical in DE: before a decision on an objection, the medical service's opinion is obtained (SGB V § 275(3b)); it advises and does not decide
* insclaim.decide, insclaim.refuse, insclaim.partial, liability.decide, totalloss.decide in US-CA: Cal. Ins. Code §§ 14020, 14021 and 14022(g): an insurer's own employees are exempt from the adjuster's licence; only an independent adjuster the insurer engages holds one. Where the insurer's own AI decides, no law of California names a person; where an independent adjuster decides, the adjuster is licensed
* insclaim.decide, insclaim.refuse, insclaim.partial, liability.decide, totalloss.decide in US-WA: WAC 284-30-330(4), as amended by WSR 26-17-089, in force from 2026-10-18: "A reasonable investigation may not rely solely on the use of a database, which includes ... estimating software and benchmarks"; it names no person

What these rules cover

These rules cover the acts of an AI in a conversation with a customer, and no other act. They send an act to a person for two reasons only: a law names a person for that act, or a trigger happened. Neither reason belongs to conversations; each applies to any act an AI does. A rule for any other kind of act would rest on the same two reasons, written in the same form.

A person affected by an act can check it: with a receipt and its signature, that STK signed it (how); with the five things a company can give, whether the rules permitted the row the company declared (how). What a receipt proves, and what it does not.

When the Rule changes

A conversation your code is in the middle of is decided by the Rule stk.py or stk.mjs holds. When STK's answer names a newer Rule, the file reads it and applies it again at once: if the newer Rule says escalate, the file returns escalate, your code hands the conversation over, and that permission is taken off the bill. From then on every ask is decided by the newer Rule. What happens when

The 6 triggers

Whatever the intent, a conversation in which one of these happened is answered escalate. Your code passes the trigger's name; it passes unknown only when none of them happened. Each one says what counts, so that no one reads it wider or narrower.

TriggerPass it when
customer_askedthe customer asked for a person (a human, an agent, a representative, a supervisor, a manager), or said they do not want to deal with the AI, in any words, once.
distressedthe customer said they are frightened, panicking, crying or cannot cope, or spoke of a medical emergency, of harming themselves, or of a danger to someone's life now.
angrythe customer insulted or swore at the company, its staff or the AI, or said they are angry or furious.
bereavementthe customer said that someone has died, or the conversation is about the account, the plan or the affairs of someone who has died.
threatthe customer threatened harm to anyone or to property, or said someone is threatening or forcing them.
legal_claimthe customer spoke of a lawyer, a lawsuit, a court, a regulator or an ombudsman, a formal complaint or a formal appeal, or of taking legal action.

The 91 intents

And 14 closed names, below the lists, each answered escalate.

What the customer asks, for each intent. Every intent here is of the domain conversation: an act of an AI in a conversation with a customer. Its full name is conversation. and the rest, as below; the rules also read it without conversation. in front.

Which version applies

The version that applies to an action is the version named in its receipt, fixed at the time STK signed it. A later version does not change the answer to an action already signed.

Laws, built differently

Laws are built differently. In US health plan rules, the law names the person who must decide. In US federal financial rules, the law sets the duty to investigate, the deadline, and the notice, but does not name a person. For financial actions a person is named by European and British law (GDPR Art. 22; UK GDPR Arts. 22A and 22C; for credit, Directive (EU) 2023/2225 Art. 18(8)) and, in the United States, from 2027-01-01, by Colorado (C.R.S. § 6-1-1705(1)(a)(II)) and California (11 CCR § 7221) for some refusals and for contesting a decision; other states' laws on credit and payments were not read. In insurance other than health, several jurisdictions license the adjuster who decides a claim. This rule puts an action on the person's side only where a person is named.

So each action below shows two things apart: the citation that names a person, which is why an action requires human review, and the clock and duties that attach to the action without naming a person.

Every change

STK's code writes every change to the history, with its date, before the changed text answers a call. The history: GET https://api.stk-evidence.com/v1/rules?history=1, no key. Every change to the rules and every report: Changelog.

Two locks

A conversation goes to a person for two reasons only: a law names a person for its act, or a trigger happened. STK's server does not start with a new version of these rules that breaks either lock.

  • Lock 1, the law. An intent is on the Never list only with a law that names a person for it: its section and the address of its official text, written beside it. An intent with no such law is not on the Never list. From the version of 2026-11-25 no intent leaves the Never list and no answer becomes less strict: STK's server does not start with a version that would.
  • Lock 2. The Triggers list can only get longer. A new version may add a trigger, never take one off or change its words. A longer list can only lower what STK is paid.

So every intent is where it is because of a law or its absence, and anyone can check each one against the official text and the reasons published with it. Only STK makes a new version; no call does.

What else decides whether STK signs

  • The limit of a day (UTC): a test key, 1,000 permissions a day; past it, STK does not sign. A live key has no limit.
  • An account whose debit was refused for good: STK signs nothing for it until it is paid. This is a condition of STK's service, in the Terms; the current text of the rules does not hold it (earlier versions had it as clause 0).
  • STK does not sign when it has no published signing key for today, while a starting server has not yet read its records in Stripe, or when it has not read from Stripe for 2 hours whether the account is unpaid. In the last two, STK answers 503: as when it cannot be reached, a grant that holds covers it.
  • When a signing key is declared invalid, every day it signed is billed nothing.
  • stk.py and stk.mjs: without an answer within 3 seconds, escalate, unless a grant holds; the same conversation and intent are not asked again the same day.
  • A grant: with each answer STK signs one for the account and the version of the rules, valid for 1 hour at most from when STK issued it. While it holds and STK cannot be reached, stk.py and stk.mjs finish what the rules say finish and keep the seal in a queue (at most 10,000 seals), then send it when STK answers again; STK signs it under the version the grant named. When the grant has expired, or the queue is full, escalate, as without a grant.
  • The seals of a day, of all accounts together, are each counted once, up to 129,138,682 in a day (UTC) (129,138,682 seals in 1408 MB, filled once on 2026-11-25 on a Mac; the next one was refused). Past that, STK does not sign a new seal that day and stk.py and stk.mjs return escalate. The seals of the day are kept in the API's memory only: when the API restarts, they are lost, and a seal signed before the restart that is sent again the same day is counted again in the count after the restart. The day is billed the larger of the counts before and after the restart, not their sum: such a seal is not billed twice, and the day can be billed less than the actions STK permitted.
  • The full texts of earlier versions are below on this page, under Every version in full, and at GET /v1/rules?history=1.
  • A key must be one of the account's current keys: keys replaced stop at once.
  • The request must carry only the seal, the time the library recorded the action and, for a seal from the queue, the grant it finished under, in at most 16,384 bytes. A grant STK did not sign for this account, an action recorded more than 30 seconds outside it (a grant lasts 1 hour at most, never past the next April 15 or October 15, 00:00 UTC, the only days a restriction takes effect; the library sets its clock only when it is more than 30 seconds from STK's), or without a grant a recorded time more than a minute from STK's clock: refused.
  • An address that sends more than 120 calls a minute with a key that is not one of STK's is answered 429 for the rest of that minute.

How a new version is published

  • Corrections, on the day they are made: a trigger added, a reason or explanation added, an error corrected.
  • The line does not change: which actions go to a person was read on 2026-11-25, from the laws named in the record. No later version moves an action to either side.

Rule 1 · adb2f2efc4e088a424b2a49b09678e3f917c75b75314570ff9464bc7ce527801

STK permission rules

These rules are the same for every company. STK answers from these rules and from nothing else: not the
words of the conversation (STK never receives them), not a confidence number.

0. Your account has an invoice still unpaid 60 days after its due date: escalate, until it is paid.
1. trigger is not unknown: escalate. (customer_asked: the customer asked for a person. angry: the customer is

No longer named by law: none

Added to the Permitted list in this version: none

Two locks. STK's server does not start with a version of these rules that breaks either:
- Lock 1, the law: an intent is on the Never list only with a law that names a person for it, its section and the
  address of its official text written beside it. An intent with no such law is not on the Never list. When that
  law stops naming a person, the version lists the intent under "No longer named by law" and it is on the
  Permitted list in that version. Every intent a version adds to the Permitted list is listed under "Added to the
  Permitted list", with its two reasons: it is not a refusal or a contest, and no law names a person for it (the
  laws checked); and whether it was taken from other.
- Lock 2: the Triggers list can only get longer: a new version may add a trigger, never take one off or change its
  words. It goes against STK's revenue: STK is paid for each permission, and a trigger only lowers their number.
So every intent is where it is because of a law or its absence, and anyone can check each one against the
official text and the reasons published with it.
Rule 6 / 2026-11-21

Rule 6 · 222b8951174827ca5e8aa3f4659984411b71ba47d0de426f9d55c93d651be8de
Published 2026-11-21 15:01:07 UTC

STK permission rules

These rules are the same for every company. STK answers from these rules and from nothing else: not the
words of the conversation (STK never receives them), not a confidence number.

Each intent is one act. read: answer what is, and change nothing. change: change something. decide: make a
decision. A conversation goes to a person for two reasons only: a law names a person for its act, or a trigger
happened. An intent is on the Never list only when a law names a person for that act; the law, its section and
the address of its official text, as STK reads them, are written beside it below. These rules are the same for
every company, so where laws differ the strictest is followed. Every other intent is on the Permitted list.

Every intent below is of the domain conversation: an act of an AI in a conversation with a customer. Its full
name is conversation. followed by the name listed (conversation.claim.status); either form is read as the same.

1. trigger is not unknown: escalate. Pass unknown only when none of the Triggers below happened in the
   conversation; when one did, pass its name.
2. intent is other: escalate. other is a conversation that could not be told as any act, so it is not known what
   it would do.
3. intent is on the Never list: escalate.
4. intent is on no list (a name these rules do not have): escalate.
5. intent is on the Closed list: escalate.
6. Otherwise: finish.

Triggers (6), each one passed when it happened at any point in the conversation, whatever the intent:
- customer_asked: the customer asked for a person (a human, an agent, a representative, a supervisor, a manager), or said they do not want to deal with the AI, in any words, once.
- distressed: the customer said they are frightened, panicking, crying or cannot cope, or spoke of a medical emergency, of harming themselves, or of a danger to someone's life now.
- angry: the customer insulted or swore at the company, its staff or the AI, or said they are angry or furious.
- bereavement: the customer said that someone has died, or the conversation is about the account, the plan or the affairs of someone who has died.
- threat: the customer threatened harm to anyone or to property, or said someone is threatening or forcing them.
- legal_claim: the customer spoke of a lawyer, a lawsuit, a court, a regulator or an ombudsman, a formal complaint or a formal appeal, or of taking legal action.

Never (17): account.refuse, claim.deny_medical, claim.refuse, collections.refuse, coverage.deny_medical, coverage.refuse, credit.refuse, decision.appeal, decision.review, dispute.refuse, fraud.refuse, limit.lower, payment_arrangement.refuse, priorauth.deny_medical, priorauth.refuse, refund.refuse, transfer.error_refuse

No longer named by law: none

Added to the Permitted list in this version: none

Two locks. STK's server does not start with a version of these rules that breaks either:
- Lock 1, the law: an intent is on the Never list only with a law that names a person for it, its section and the
  address of its official text written beside it. An intent with no such law is not on the Never list. When that
  law stops naming a person, the version lists the intent under "No longer named by law" and it is on the
  Permitted list in that version. Every intent a version adds to the Permitted list is listed under "Added to the
  Permitted list", with its two reasons: it is not a refusal or a contest, and no law names a person for it (the
  laws checked); and whether it was taken from other.
- Lock 2: the Triggers list can only get longer: a new version may add a trigger, never take one off or change its
  words. It goes against STK's revenue: STK is paid for each permission, and a trigger only lowers their number.
So every intent is where it is because of a law or its absence, and anyone can check each one against the
official text and the reasons published with it.
Rule 7 / 2026-11-22

Rule 7 · 5555868c654de0b9403056f93d67c96690936844a030ee371516ef156209ca65
Published 2026-11-22 10:53:40 UTC

STK permission rules

These rules are the same for every company. STK answers from these rules and from nothing else: not the
words of the conversation (STK never receives them), not a confidence number.

Each intent is one act. read: answer what is, and change nothing. change: change something. decide: make a
decision. A conversation goes to a person for two reasons only: a law names a person for its act, or a trigger
happened. An intent is on the Never list only when a law names a person for that act; the law, its section and
the address of its official text, as STK reads them, are written beside it below. These rules are the same for
every company, so where laws differ the strictest is followed. Every other intent is on the Permitted list.

Every intent below is of the domain conversation: an act of an AI in a conversation with a customer. Its full
name is conversation. followed by the name listed (conversation.claim.status); either form is read as the same.

1. trigger is not unknown: escalate. Pass unknown only when none of the Triggers below happened in the
   conversation; when one did, pass its name.
2. intent is other: escalate. other is a conversation that could not be told as any act, so it is not known what
   it would do.
3. intent is on the Never list: escalate.
4. intent is on no list (a name these rules do not have): escalate.
5. intent is on the Closed list: escalate.
6. Otherwise: finish.

Triggers (6), each one passed when it happened at any point in the conversation, whatever the intent:
- customer_asked: the customer asked for a person (a human, an agent, a representative, a supervisor, a manager), or said they do not want to deal with the AI, in any words, once.
- distressed: the customer said they are frightened, panicking, crying or cannot cope, or spoke of a medical emergency, of harming themselves, or of a danger to someone's life now.
- angry: the customer insulted or swore at the company, its staff or the AI, or said they are angry or furious.
- bereavement: the customer said that someone has died, or the conversation is about the account, the plan or the affairs of someone who has died.
- threat: the customer threatened harm to anyone or to property, or said someone is threatening or forcing them.
- legal_claim: the customer spoke of a lawyer, a lawsuit, a court, a regulator or an ombudsman, a formal complaint or a formal appeal, or of taking legal action.

Never (17): account.refuse, claim.deny_medical, claim.refuse, collections.refuse, coverage.deny_medical, coverage.refuse, credit.refuse, decision.appeal, decision.review, dispute.refuse, fraud.refuse, limit.lower, payment_arrangement.refuse, priorauth.deny_medical, priorauth.refuse, refund.refuse, transfer.error_refuse

No longer named by law: none

Added to the Permitted list in this version: none

Two locks. STK's server does not start with a version of these rules that breaks either:
- Lock 1, the law: an intent is on the Never list only with a law that names a person for it, its section and the
  address of its official text written beside it. An intent with no such law is not on the Never list. When that
  law stops naming a person, the version lists the intent under "No longer named by law" and it is on the
  Permitted list in that version. Every intent a version adds to the Permitted list is listed under "Added to the
  Permitted list", with its two reasons: it is not a refusal or a contest, and no law names a person for it (the
  laws checked); and whether it was taken from other.
- Lock 2: the Triggers list can only get longer: a new version may add a trigger, never take one off or change its
  words. It goes against STK's revenue: STK is paid for each permission, and a trigger only lowers their number.
So every intent is where it is because of a law or its absence, and anyone can check each one against the
official text and the reasons published with it.
Rule 8 / 2026-11-22

Rule 8 · 458ddd6bea60560c9e063af86976e5e4941f97ef49a7b6a09a7bdc053b7ea38e
Published 2026-11-22 14:28:30 UTC

STK permission rules

These rules are the same for every company. STK answers from these rules and from nothing else: not the
words of the conversation (STK never receives them), not a confidence number.

Each intent is one act. read: answer what is, and change nothing. change: change something. decide: make a
decision. A conversation goes to a person for two reasons only: a law names a person for its act, or a trigger
happened. An intent is on the Never list only when a law names a person for that act; the law, its section and
the address of its official text, as STK reads them, are written beside it below. These rules are the same for
every company, so where laws differ the strictest is followed. Every other intent is on the Permitted list.

Every intent below is of the domain conversation: an act of an AI in a conversation with a customer. Its full
name is conversation. followed by the name listed (conversation.claim.status); either form is read as the same.

1. trigger is not unknown: escalate. Pass unknown only when none of the Triggers below happened in the
   conversation; when one did, pass its name.
2. intent is other: escalate. other is a conversation that could not be told as any act, so it is not known what
   it would do.
3. intent is on the Never list: escalate.
4. intent is on no list (a name these rules do not have): escalate.
5. intent is on the Closed list: escalate.
6. Otherwise: finish.

Triggers (6), each one passed when it happened at any point in the conversation, whatever the intent:
- customer_asked: the customer asked for a person (a human, an agent, a representative, a supervisor, a manager), or said they do not want to deal with the AI, in any words, once.
- distressed: the customer said they are frightened, panicking, crying or cannot cope, or spoke of a medical emergency, of harming themselves, or of a danger to someone's life now.
- angry: the customer insulted or swore at the company, its staff or the AI, or said they are angry or furious.
- bereavement: the customer said that someone has died, or the conversation is about the account, the plan or the affairs of someone who has died.
- threat: the customer threatened harm to anyone or to property, or said someone is threatening or forcing them.
- legal_claim: the customer spoke of a lawyer, a lawsuit, a court, a regulator or an ombudsman, a formal complaint or a formal appeal, or of taking legal action.

Never (17): account.refuse, claim.deny_medical, claim.refuse, collections.refuse, coverage.deny_medical, coverage.refuse, credit.refuse, decision.appeal, decision.review, dispute.refuse, fraud.refuse, limit.lower, payment_arrangement.refuse, priorauth.deny_medical, priorauth.refuse, refund.refuse, transfer.error_refuse

No longer named by law: none

Added to the Permitted list in this version: none

Two locks. STK's server does not start with a version of these rules that breaks either:
- Lock 1, the law: an intent is on the Never list only with a law that names a person for it, its section and the
  address of its official text written beside it. An intent with no such law is not on the Never list. When that
  law stops naming a person, the version lists the intent under "No longer named by law" and it is on the
  Permitted list in that version. Every intent a version adds to the Permitted list is listed under "Added to the
  Permitted list", with its two reasons: it is not a refusal or a contest, and no law names a person for it (the
  laws checked); and whether it was taken from other.
- Lock 2: the Triggers list can only get longer: a new version may add a trigger, never take one off or change its
  words. It goes against STK's revenue: STK is paid for each permission, and a trigger only lowers their number.
So every intent is where it is because of a law or its absence, and anyone can check each one against the
official text and the reasons published with it.
Rule 9 / 2026-11-23

Rule 9 · 33ddd43487c5c40a928d55632b75c305cac632da09a3ebf376427e4ff0d3c8aa
Published 2026-11-23 05:56:32 UTC

STK permission rules

These rules are the same for every company. STK answers from these rules and from nothing else: not the
words of the conversation (STK never receives them), not a confidence number.

Each intent is one act. read: answer what is, and change nothing. change: change something. decide: make a
decision. A conversation goes to a person for two reasons only: a law names a person for its act, or a trigger
happened. An intent is on the Never list only when a law names a person for that act; the law, its section and
the address of its official text, as STK reads them, are written beside it below. Every other intent is on the
Permitted list. When no jurisdiction is given, or one whose laws on the subject of the intent have not been read
(the Read list below), the strictest is followed: an intent on the Never list goes to a person. When jurisdictions
are given whose laws on its subject have been read, an intent on the Never list goes to a person only where a law
of one of them, written beside it below, names a person for it.

Every intent below is of the domain conversation: an act of an AI in a conversation with a customer. Its full
name is conversation. followed by the name listed (conversation.claim.status); either form is read as the same.

1. trigger is not unknown: escalate. Pass unknown only when none of the Triggers below happened in the
   conversation; when one did, pass its name.
2. intent is other: escalate. other is a conversation that could not be told as any act, so it is not known what
   it would do.
3. intent is on the Never list: escalate; when jurisdictions read for its subject are given, only if a law of
   one of them names a person for it.
4. intent is on no list (a name these rules do not have): escalate.
5. intent is on the Closed list: escalate.
6. Otherwise: finish.

Triggers (6), each one passed when it happened at any point in the conversation, whatever the intent:
- customer_asked: the customer asked for a person (a human, an agent, a representative, a supervisor, a manager), or said they do not want to deal with the AI, in any words, once.
- distressed: the customer said they are frightened, panicking, crying or cannot cope, or spoke of a medical emergency, of harming themselves, or of a danger to someone's life now.
- angry: the customer insulted or swore at the company, its staff or the AI, or said they are angry or furious.
- bereavement: the customer said that someone has died, or the conversation is about the account, the plan or the affairs of someone who has died.
- threat: the customer threatened harm to anyone or to property, or said someone is threatening or forcing them.
- legal_claim: the customer spoke of a lawyer, a lawsuit, a court, a regulator or an ombudsman, a formal complaint or a formal appeal, or of taking legal action.

Never (17): account.refuse, claim.deny_medical, claim.refuse, collections.refuse, coverage.deny_medical, coverage.refuse, credit.refuse, decision.appeal, decision.review, dispute.refuse, fraud.refuse, limit.lower, payment_arrangement.refuse, priorauth.deny_medical, priorauth.refuse, refund.refuse, transfer.error_refuse

Two locks. STK's server does not start with a version of these rules that breaks either:
- Lock 1, the law: an intent is on the Never list only with a law that names a person for it, its section and the
  address of its official text written beside it. An intent with no such law is not on the Never list. When that
  law stops naming a person, the version lists the intent under "No longer named by law" and it is on the
  Permitted list in that version. Every intent a version adds to the Permitted list is listed under "Added to the
  Permitted list", with its two reasons: it is not a refusal or a contest, and no law names a person for it (the
  laws checked); and whether it was taken from other. For each jurisdiction read, an intent goes to a person in
  it only with a law of that jurisdiction written beside it, and leaves only by naming the law that stopped.
- Lock 2: the Triggers list can only get longer: a new version may add a trigger, never take one off or change its
  words. It goes against STK's revenue: STK is paid for each permission, and a trigger only lowers their number.
So every intent is where it is because of a law or its absence, and anyone can check each one against the
official text and the reasons published with it.
Rule 10 / 2026-11-23

Rule 10 · 4ee31e3ad2950eb686cbe55fba16dbabeddc1bf748d63c50467eb531132adc0c
Published 2026-11-23 07:00:07 UTC

STK permission rules

These rules are the same for every company. STK answers from these rules and from nothing else: not the
words of the conversation (STK never receives them), not a confidence number.

Each intent is one act. read: answer what is, and change nothing. change: change something. decide: make a
decision. A conversation goes to a person for two reasons only: a law names a person for its act, or a trigger
happened. An intent is on the Never list only when a law names a person for that act; the law, its section and
the address of its official text, as STK reads them, are written beside it below. Every other intent is on the
Permitted list. When no jurisdiction is given, or one whose laws on the subject of the intent are not read (the
Checked list below), the strictest is followed: an intent on the Never list goes to a person when a law beside it
applies on the day. When jurisdictions are given whose laws on its subject are read, an intent on the Never list
goes to a person only where a law of one of them, written beside it below, names a person for it and applies on
the day.

Every intent below is of the domain conversation: an act of an AI in a conversation with a customer. Its full
name is conversation. followed by the name listed (conversation.claim.status); either form is read as the same.

1. trigger is not unknown: escalate. Pass unknown only when none of the Triggers below happened in the
   conversation; when one did, pass its name.
2. intent is other: escalate. other is a conversation that could not be told as any act, so it is not known what
   it would do.
3. intent is on the Never list and a law beside it applies on the day: escalate; when jurisdictions read for its
   subject are given, only if such a law is one of theirs.
4. intent is on no list (a name these rules do not have): escalate.
5. intent is on the Closed list: escalate.
6. Otherwise: finish.

Triggers (6), each one passed when it happened at any point in the conversation, whatever the intent:
- customer_asked: the customer asked for a person (a human, an agent, a representative, a supervisor, a manager), or said they do not want to deal with the AI, in any words, once.
- distressed: the customer said they are frightened, panicking, crying or cannot cope, or spoke of a medical emergency, of harming themselves, or of a danger to someone's life now.
- angry: the customer insulted or swore at the company, its staff or the AI, or said they are angry or furious.
- bereavement: the customer said that someone has died, or the conversation is about the account, the plan or the affairs of someone who has died.
- threat: the customer threatened harm to anyone or to property, or said someone is threatening or forcing them.
- legal_claim: the customer spoke of a lawyer, a lawsuit, a court, a regulator or an ombudsman, a formal complaint or a formal appeal, or of taking legal action.

Never (17): account.refuse, claim.deny_medical, claim.refuse, collections.refuse, coverage.deny_medical, coverage.refuse, credit.refuse, decision.appeal, decision.review, dispute.refuse, fraud.refuse, limit.lower, payment_arrangement.refuse, priorauth.deny_medical, priorauth.refuse, refund.refuse, transfer.error_refuse

(US-WA), EU for the European Union; UK is read as GB. A code takes in the laws of what it is part or member of,
and a country's code the laws of its parts (the lists below): US is the laws of the United States and of each
state; US-WA, of the United States and of Washington; DE, of the EU and of Germany; EU, of the EU. Where several

Days. A law applies from the day written beside its jurisdiction below (00:00 UTC), and from the day it is cited

not beside it.

Two locks. STK's server does not start with a version of these rules that breaks either:
- Lock 1, the law: an intent is on the Never list only with a law that names a person for it, its section and the
  address of its official text written beside it. An intent with no such law is not on the Never list. When that
  law stops naming a person, the version lists the intent under "No longer named by law" and it is on the
  Permitted list in that version. Every intent a version adds to the Permitted list is listed under "Added to the
  Permitted list", with its two reasons: it is not a refusal or a contest, and no law names a person for it (the
  laws checked); and whether it was taken from other. For each jurisdiction read, an intent goes to a person in
  it only with a law of that jurisdiction written beside it, and leaves only by naming the law that stopped.
- Lock 2: the Triggers list can only get longer: a new version may add a trigger, never take one off or change its
  words. It goes against STK's revenue: STK is paid for each permission, and a trigger only lowers their number.
So every intent is where it is because of a law or its absence, and anyone can check each one against the
official text and the reasons published with it.

Rule 11 · e4fd50464c7fd68b441f2c8502557cc61e4039b48aa15da33aa75e7bc5836483
Published 2026-11-23 07:25:57 UTC

STK permission rules

These rules are the same for every company. STK answers from these rules and from nothing else: not the
words of the conversation (STK never receives them), not a confidence number.

Each intent is one act. read: answer what is, and change nothing. change: change something. decide: make a
decision. A conversation goes to a person for two reasons only: a law names a person for its act, or a trigger
happened. An intent is on the Never list only when a law names a person for that act; the law, its section and
the address of its official text, as STK reads them, are written beside it below. Every other intent is on the
Permitted list. When no jurisdiction is given, or one whose laws on the subject of the intent are not read (the
Checked list below), the strictest is followed: an intent on the Never list goes to a person when a law beside it
applies on the day. When jurisdictions are given whose laws on its subject are read, an intent on the Never list
goes to a person only where a law of one of them, written beside it below, names a person for it and applies on
the day.

Every intent below is of the domain conversation: an act of an AI in a conversation with a customer. Its full
name is conversation. followed by the name listed (conversation.claim.status); either form is read as the same.

1. trigger is not unknown: escalate. Pass unknown only when none of the Triggers below happened in the
   conversation; when one did, pass its name.
2. intent is other: escalate. other is a conversation that could not be told as any act, so it is not known what
   it would do.
3. intent is on the Never list and a law beside it applies on the day: escalate; when jurisdictions read for its
   subject are given, only if such a law is one of theirs.
4. intent is on no list (a name these rules do not have): escalate.
5. intent is on the Closed list: escalate.
6. Otherwise: finish.

Triggers (6), each one passed when it happened at any point in the conversation, whatever the intent:
- customer_asked: the customer asked for a person (a human, an agent, a representative, a supervisor, a manager), or said they do not want to deal with the AI, in any words, once.
- distressed: the customer said they are frightened, panicking, crying or cannot cope, or spoke of a medical emergency, of harming themselves, or of a danger to someone's life now.
- angry: the customer insulted or swore at the company, its staff or the AI, or said they are angry or furious.
- bereavement: the customer said that someone has died, or the conversation is about the account, the plan or the affairs of someone who has died.
- threat: the customer threatened harm to anyone or to property, or said someone is threatening or forcing them.
- legal_claim: the customer spoke of a lawyer, a lawsuit, a court, a regulator or an ombudsman, a formal complaint or a formal appeal, or of taking legal action.

Two locks. STK's server does not start with a version of these rules that breaks either:
- Lock 1, the law: an intent is on the Never list only with a law that names a person for it, its section and the
  address of its official text written beside it. An intent with no such law is not on the Never list. When that
  law stops naming a person, the version lists the intent under "No longer named by law" and it is on the
  Permitted list in that version. Every intent a version adds to the Permitted list is listed under "Added to the
  Permitted list", with its two reasons: it is not a refusal or a contest, and no law names a person for it (the
  laws checked); and whether it was taken from other. For each jurisdiction read, an intent goes to a person in
  it only with a law of that jurisdiction written beside it, and leaves only by naming the law that stopped.
- Lock 2: the Triggers list can only get longer: a new version may add a trigger, never take one off or change its
  words. It goes against STK's revenue: STK is paid for each permission, and a trigger only lowers their number.
So every intent is where it is because of a law or its absence, and anyone can check each one against the
official text and the reasons published with it.

Rule 12 · ae62d379c12db97e79a24d1b7585233f0eb8a63b2595b44955e641cd55f7b2d5
Published 2026-11-23 08:03:03 UTC

STK permission rules

These rules are the same for every company. STK answers from these rules and from nothing else: not the
words of the conversation (STK never receives them), not a confidence number.

Each intent is one act. read: answer what is, and change nothing. change: change something. decide: make a
decision. A conversation goes to a person for two reasons only: a law names a person for its act, or a trigger
happened. An intent is on the Never list only when a law names a person for that act; the law, its section and
the address of its official text, as STK reads them, are written beside it below. Every other intent is on the
Permitted list. When no jurisdiction is given, or one whose laws on the subject of the intent are not read (the
Checked list below), the strictest is followed: an intent on the Never list goes to a person when a law beside it
applies on the day. When jurisdictions are given whose laws on its subject are read, an intent on the Never list
goes to a person only where a law of one of them, written beside it below, names a person for it and applies on
the day.

Every intent below is of the domain conversation: an act of an AI in a conversation with a customer. Its full
name is conversation. followed by the name listed (conversation.claim.status); either form is read as the same.

1. trigger is not unknown: escalate. Pass unknown only when none of the Triggers below happened in the
   conversation; when one did, pass its name.
2. intent is other: escalate. other is a conversation that could not be told as any act, so it is not known what
   it would do.
3. intent is on the Never list and a law beside it applies on the day: escalate; when jurisdictions read for its
   subject are given, only if such a law is one of theirs.
4. intent is on no list (a name these rules do not have): escalate.
5. intent is on the Closed list: escalate.
6. Otherwise: finish.

Triggers (6), each one passed when it happened at any point in the conversation, whatever the intent:
- customer_asked: the customer asked for a person (a human, an agent, a representative, a supervisor, a manager), or said they do not want to deal with the AI, in any words, once.
- distressed: the customer said they are frightened, panicking, crying or cannot cope, or spoke of a medical emergency, of harming themselves, or of a danger to someone's life now.
- angry: the customer insulted or swore at the company, its staff or the AI, or said they are angry or furious.
- bereavement: the customer said that someone has died, or the conversation is about the account, the plan or the affairs of someone who has died.
- threat: the customer threatened harm to anyone or to property, or said someone is threatening or forcing them.
- legal_claim: the customer spoke of a lawyer, a lawsuit, a court, a regulator or an ombudsman, a formal complaint or a formal appeal, or of taking legal action.

Never (17): account.refuse, claim.deny_medical, claim.refuse, collections.refuse, coverage.deny_medical, coverage.refuse, credit.refuse, decision.appeal, decision.review, dispute.refuse, fraud.refuse, limit.lower, payment_arrangement.refuse, priorauth.deny_medical, priorauth.refuse, refund.refuse, transfer.error_refuse

The law that names a person, for each intent on the Never list:
- account.refuse: GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) Art. 22(1) and (3); UK GDPR Arts. 22A and 22C; C.R.S. § 6-1-1705(1)(a)(II) (Colorado SB 26-189: on the consumer's request, the deployer provides an opportunity for meaningful human review and reconsideration of the consequential decision, to the extent commercially reasonable; definitions in § 6-1-1701(15); applies to decisions made on or after 2027-01-01; enforcement stayed by the order of 2026-04-27 in X.AI LLC v. Weiser, No. 1:26-cv-01515 (D. Colo.); the attorney general's rules, 4 CCR 904-6, not in effect); 11 CCR § 7221(a), (b)(1)(A) (California, regulations under the CCPA: the business provides the consumer with a method to appeal the decision to a human reviewer who has the authority to overturn the decision; for decisions on financial or lending services, § 7001(ddd)(1); from 2027-01-01; not automated decisionmaking technology where the human involvement of § 7001(e)(1) is present; decisions of a financial institution on consumers' nonpublic personal information may be outside it by the exemption for GLBA data in Cal. Jurisdictions. Each is given by its code: ISO 3166-1 for a country (US, GB), ISO 3166-2 for a part of one
(US-WA), EU for the European Union; UK is read as GB. A code takes in the laws of what it is part or member of,
and a country's code the laws of its parts (the lists below): US is the laws of the United States and of each
state; US-WA, of the United States and of Washington; DE, of the EU and of Germany; EU, of the EU. Where several
are given, each is applied and the strictest is followed.

Days. A law applies from the day written beside its jurisdiction below (00:00 UTC), and from the day it is cited
when none is written. Before that day it sends no intent to a person; the intent is answered as if that law were
not beside it.

Where each law beside an intent on the Never list applies, and from when (US alone: a law of the United States):

L315-1, L315-2; KVG Art. 57, 58; Private Health Insurance Act 2007 s 75-15. Each citation says whom

Two locks. STK's server does not start with a version of these rules that breaks either:
- Lock 1, the law: an intent is on the Never list only with a law that names a person for it, its section and the
  address of its official text written beside it. An intent with no such law is not on the Never list. When that
  law stops naming a person, the version lists the intent under "No longer named by law" and it is on the
  Permitted list in that version. Every intent a version adds to the Permitted list is listed under "Added to the
  Permitted list", with its two reasons: it is not a refusal or a contest, and no law names a person for it (the
  laws checked); and whether it was taken from other. For each jurisdiction read, an intent goes to a person in
  it only with a law of that jurisdiction written beside it, and leaves only by naming the law that stopped.
- Lock 2: the Triggers list can only get longer: a new version may add a trigger, never take one off or change its
  words. It goes against STK's revenue: STK is paid for each permission, and a trigger only lowers their number.
So every intent is where it is because of a law or its absence, and anyone can check each one against the
official text and the reasons published with it.

Rule 13 · f426107a05ccb51aa09cae154735ad8fe932269b7ebd1d656fa6c639331a0739
Published 2026-11-23 09:38:22 UTC

STK permission rules

These rules are the same for every company. STK answers from these rules and from nothing else: not the
words of the conversation (STK never receives them), not a confidence number.

Each intent is one act. read: answer what is, and change nothing. change: change something. decide: make a
decision. A conversation goes to a person for two reasons only: a law names a person for its act, or a trigger
happened. An intent is on the Never list only when a law names a person for that act; the law, its section and
the address of its official text, as STK reads them, are written beside it below. Every other intent is on the
Permitted list. When no jurisdiction is given, or one whose laws on the subject of the intent are not read (the
Checked list below), the strictest is followed: an intent on the Never list goes to a person when a law beside it
applies on the day. When jurisdictions are given whose laws on its subject are read, an intent on the Never list
goes to a person only where a law of one of them, written beside it below, names a person for it and applies on
the day.

Every intent below is of the domain conversation: an act of an AI in a conversation with a customer. Its full
name is conversation. followed by the name listed (conversation.claim.status); either form is read as the same.

1. trigger is not unknown: escalate. Pass unknown only when none of the Triggers below happened in the
   conversation; when one did, pass its name.
2. intent is other: escalate. other is a conversation that could not be told as any act, so it is not known what
   it would do.
3. intent is on the Never list and a law beside it applies on the day: escalate; when jurisdictions read for its
   subject are given, only if such a law is one of theirs.
4. intent is on no list (a name these rules do not have): escalate.
5. intent is on the Closed list: escalate.
6. Otherwise: finish.

Triggers (6), each one passed when it happened at any point in the conversation, whatever the intent:
- customer_asked: the customer asked for a person (a human, an agent, a representative, a supervisor, a manager), or said they do not want to deal with the AI, in any words, once.
- distressed: the customer said they are frightened, panicking, crying or cannot cope, or spoke of a medical emergency, of harming themselves, or of a danger to someone's life now.
- angry: the customer insulted or swore at the company, its staff or the AI, or said they are angry or furious.
- bereavement: the customer said that someone has died, or the conversation is about the account, the plan or the affairs of someone who has died.
- threat: the customer threatened harm to anyone or to property, or said someone is threatening or forcing them.
- legal_claim: the customer spoke of a lawyer, a lawsuit, a court, a regulator or an ombudsman, a formal complaint or a formal appeal, or of taking legal action.

Never (17): account.refuse, claim.deny_medical, claim.refuse, collections.refuse, coverage.deny_medical, coverage.refuse, credit.refuse, decision.appeal, decision.review, dispute.refuse, fraud.refuse, limit.lower, payment_arrangement.refuse, priorauth.deny_medical, priorauth.refuse, refund.refuse, transfer.error_refuse

Jurisdictions. Each is given by its code: ISO 3166-1 for a country (US, GB), ISO 3166-2 for a part of one
(US-WA), EU for the European Union; UK is read as GB. A code takes in the laws of what it is part or member of,
and a country's code the laws of its parts (the lists below): US is the laws of the United States and of each
state; US-WA, of the United States and of Washington; DE, of the EU and of Germany; EU, of the EU. Where several
are given, each is applied and the strictest is followed.

Days. A law applies from the day written beside its jurisdiction below (00:00 UTC), and from the day it is cited
when none is written. Before that day it sends no intent to a person; the intent is answered as if that law were
not beside it.

Three kinds of law put an intent on the Never list, each counted in these rules as a law that names a person for it:
- A, a qualified person: a law names who decides by licence or qualification: a physician, a clinical peer, a medical director, a médico, a praticien conseil, a Vertrauensarzt, a medical practitioner. Most laws of the United States beside health intents; ANS Resolução Normativa nº 424/2017; Code de la sécurité sociale, art. L315-1, L315-2; KVG Art. 57, 58; Private Health Insurance Act 2007 s 75-15. Each citation says whom
- B, a right on request: a person may ask for a human review of a decision: UK GDPR Art. 22C; C.R.S. § 6-1-1705(1)(a)(II); 11 CCR § 7221
- C, a category of decision: a law requires the first decision to be taken by a person because of what is decided, with no request and no licence: GDPR Art. 22(1) and (4), a prohibition in principle that need not be invoked (CJEU C-634/21, SCHUFA, 2023-12-07), unless Art. 22(2) applies; UK GDPR Art. 22B, for special categories of personal data, unless its conditions are met; the IRDAI Master Circular on Health Insurance Business, para. 17(a), a committee; O.C.G.A. § 33-46-7.1(c) (Georgia SB 444, from 2027-01-01), an AI tool that is not the sole basis of an adverse determination and does not supersede the clinical peer's judgment

Two locks. STK's server does not start with a version of these rules that breaks either:
- Lock 1, the law: an intent is on the Never list only with a law that names a person for it, its section and the
  address of its official text written beside it. An intent with no such law is not on the Never list. When that
  law stops naming a person, the version lists the intent under "No longer named by law" and it is on the
  Permitted list in that version. Every intent a version adds to the Permitted list is listed under "Added to the
  Permitted list", with its two reasons: it is not a refusal or a contest, and no law names a person for it (the
  laws checked); and whether it was taken from other. For each jurisdiction read, an intent goes to a person in
  it only with a law of that jurisdiction written beside it, and leaves only by naming the law that stopped.
- Lock 2: the Triggers list can only get longer: a new version may add a trigger, never take one off or change its
  words. It goes against STK's revenue: STK is paid for each permission, and a trigger only lowers their number.
So every intent is where it is because of a law or its absence, and anyone can check each one against the
official text and the reasons published with it.

Rule 14 · 22ddf282ece83cc9706db67bd83d84233ea31104993b5e9e118cfe4033ab71c3
Published 2026-11-23 10:56:55 UTC

STK permission rules

These rules are the same for every company. STK answers from these rules and from nothing else: not the
words of the conversation (STK never receives them), not a confidence number.

Each intent is one act. read: answer what is, and change nothing. change: change something. decide: make a
decision. A conversation goes to a person for two reasons only: a law names a person for its act, or a trigger
happened. An intent is on the Never list only when a law names a person for that act; the law, its section and
the address of its official text, as STK reads them, are written beside it below. Every other intent is on the
Permitted list. When no jurisdiction is given, or one whose laws on the subject of the intent are not read (the
Checked list below), the strictest is followed: an intent on the Never list goes to a person when a law beside it
applies on the day. When jurisdictions are given whose laws on its subject are read, an intent on the Never list
goes to a person only where a law of one of them, written beside it below, names a person for it and applies on
the day.

Every intent below is of the domain conversation: an act of an AI in a conversation with a customer. Its full
name is conversation. followed by the name listed (conversation.claim.status); either form is read as the same.

1. trigger is not unknown: escalate. Pass unknown only when none of the Triggers below happened in the
   conversation; when one did, pass its name.
2. intent is other: escalate. other is a conversation that could not be told as any act, so it is not known what
   it would do.
3. intent is on the Never list and a law beside it applies on the day: escalate; when jurisdictions read for its
   subject are given, only if such a law is one of theirs.
4. intent is on no list (a name these rules do not have): escalate.
5. intent is on the Closed list: escalate.
6. Otherwise: finish.

Triggers (6), each one passed when it happened at any point in the conversation, whatever the intent:
- customer_asked: the customer asked for a person (a human, an agent, a representative, a supervisor, a manager), or said they do not want to deal with the AI, in any words, once.
- distressed: the customer said they are frightened, panicking, crying or cannot cope, or spoke of a medical emergency, of harming themselves, or of a danger to someone's life now.
- angry: the customer insulted or swore at the company, its staff or the AI, or said they are angry or furious.
- bereavement: the customer said that someone has died, or the conversation is about the account, the plan or the affairs of someone who has died.
- threat: the customer threatened harm to anyone or to property, or said someone is threatening or forcing them.
- legal_claim: the customer spoke of a lawyer, a lawsuit, a court, a regulator or an ombudsman, a formal complaint or a formal appeal, or of taking legal action.

Jurisdictions. Each is given by its code: ISO 3166-1 for a country (US, GB), ISO 3166-2 for a part of one
(US-WA), EU for the European Union; UK is read as GB. A code takes in the laws of what it is part or member of,
and a country's code the laws of its parts (the lists below): US is the laws of the United States and of each
state; US-WA, of the United States and of Washington; DE, of the EU and of Germany; EU, of the EU. Where several
are given, each is applied and the strictest is followed.

Days. A law applies from the day written beside its jurisdiction below (00:00 UTC), and from the day it is cited
when none is written. Before that day it sends no intent to a person; the intent is answered as if that law were
not beside it.

Two locks. STK's server does not start with a version of these rules that breaks either:
- Lock 1, the law: an intent is on the Never list only with a law that names a person for it, its section and the
  address of its official text written beside it. An intent with no such law is not on the Never list. When that
  law stops naming a person, the version lists the intent under "No longer named by law" and it is on the
  Permitted list in that version. Every intent a version adds to the Permitted list is listed under "Added to the
  Permitted list", with its two reasons: it is not a refusal or a contest, and no law names a person for it (the
  laws checked); and whether it was taken from other. For each jurisdiction read, an intent goes to a person in
  it only with a law of that jurisdiction written beside it, and leaves only by naming the law that stopped.
- Lock 2: the Triggers list can only get longer: a new version may add a trigger, never take one off or change its
  words. It goes against STK's revenue: STK is paid for each permission, and a trigger only lowers their number.
So every intent is where it is because of a law or its absence, and anyone can check each one against the
official text and the reasons published with it.

Rule 15 · 4bbb7c956c5777200aae63a0a006b922b36ce5fe18765c96c37c12af1305c710
Published 2026-11-24 02:50:44 UTC

STK permission rules

These rules are the same for every company. STK answers from these rules and from nothing else: not the
words of the conversation (STK never receives them), not a confidence number.

Each intent is one act. read: answer what is, and change nothing. change: change something. decide: make a
decision. A conversation goes to a person for two reasons only: a law names a person for its act, or a trigger
happened. An intent is on the Never list only when a law names a person for that act; the law, its section and
the address of its official text, as STK reads them, are written beside it below. Every other intent is on the
Permitted list. When no jurisdiction is given, the strictest is followed: an intent on the Never list goes to a
person when a law beside it applies on the day, in any jurisdiction. When jurisdictions are given, an intent on the
Never list goes to a person only where a law of one of them, written beside it below, names a person for it and
applies on the day; where none is written, it is finished, whether or not that jurisdiction's laws have been read.

The Checked list places no intent.
Whether a jurisdiction's laws have been read (the Checked list below) is written in each row asked with it and shown
on the site. It sends no intent to a person and takes none from one.

Every intent below is of the domain conversation: an act of an AI in a conversation with a customer. Its full
name is conversation. followed by the name listed (conversation.claim.status); either form is read as the same.

1. trigger is not unknown: escalate. Pass unknown only when none of the Triggers below happened in the
   conversation; when one did, pass its name.
2. intent is other: escalate. other is a conversation that could not be told as any act, so it is not known what
   it would do.
3. intent is on the Never list and a law beside it applies on the day: escalate; when jurisdictions are given,
   only if such a law is one of theirs.
4. intent is on no list (a name these rules do not have): escalate.
5. intent is on the Closed list: escalate.
6. Otherwise: finish.

Triggers (6), each one passed when it happened at any point in the conversation, whatever the intent:
- customer_asked: the customer asked for a person (a human, an agent, a representative, a supervisor, a manager), or said they do not want to deal with the AI, in any words, once.
- distressed: the customer said they are frightened, panicking, crying or cannot cope, or spoke of a medical emergency, of harming themselves, or of a danger to someone's life now.
- angry: the customer insulted or swore at the company, its staff or the AI, or said they are angry or furious.
- bereavement: the customer said that someone has died, or the conversation is about the account, the plan or the affairs of someone who has died.
- threat: the customer threatened harm to anyone or to property, or said someone is threatening or forcing them.
- legal_claim: the customer spoke of a lawyer, a lawsuit, a court, a regulator or an ombudsman, a formal complaint or a formal appeal, or of taking legal action.

Two locks. STK's server does not start with a version of these rules that breaks either:
- Lock 1, the law: an intent is on the Never list only with a law that names a person for it, its section and the
  address of its official text written beside it. An intent with no such law is not on the Never list. When that
  law stops naming a person, the version lists the intent under "No longer named by law" and it is on the
  Permitted list in that version. Every intent a version adds to the Permitted list is listed under "Added to the
  Permitted list", with its two reasons: it is not a refusal or a contest, and no law names a person for it (the
  laws checked); and whether it was taken from other. In each jurisdiction, read or not, an intent goes to a person
  only with a law of that jurisdiction, of kind A, B or C, written beside it and applying on the day; a law not
  found is no law. It leaves only by naming the law that stopped.
- Lock 2: the Triggers list can only get longer: a new version may add a trigger, never take one off or change its
  words. It goes against STK's revenue: STK is paid for each permission, and a trigger only lowers their number.
So every intent is where it is because of a law or its absence, and anyone can check each one against the
official text and the reasons published with it.
Rule 16 / 2026-11-24

Rule 16 · 6a6eae6c67d9f3a7adc8dfee49b5cbafc8d92f8a83e386973ae895340a9655eb
Published 2026-11-24 15:00:25 UTC

STK permission rules

These rules are the same for every company. STK answers from these rules and from nothing else: not the
words of the conversation (STK never receives them), not a confidence number.

Each intent is one act. read: answer what is, and change nothing. change: change something. decide: make a
decision. A conversation goes to a person for two reasons only: a law names a person for its act, or a trigger
happened. An intent is on the Never list only when a law names a person for that act; the law, its section and
the address of its official text, as STK reads them, are written beside it below. Every other intent is on the
Permitted list. When no jurisdiction is given, the strictest is followed: an intent on the Never list goes to a
person when a law beside it applies on the day, in any jurisdiction. When jurisdictions are given, an intent on the
Never list goes to a person only where a law of one of them, written beside it below, names a person for it and
applies on the day; where none is written, it is finished, if that jurisdiction's laws on the intent's subject have
been read (the Checked list below). A jurisdiction whose laws on it have not been read is answered as if none were
given: the strictest, a person only by a law written beside the intent.

The Checked list places no intent.
A jurisdiction not on the Checked list for the subject of an intent is answered as if none were given.
Whether a jurisdiction's laws have been read (the Checked list below) is written in each row asked with it and shown
on the site. It sends no intent to a person and takes none from one.

Every intent below is of the domain conversation: an act of an AI in a conversation with a customer. Its full
name is conversation. followed by the name listed (conversation.claim.status); either form is read as the same.

1. trigger is not unknown: escalate. Pass unknown only when none of the Triggers below happened in the
   conversation; when one did, pass its name.
2. intent is other: escalate. other is a conversation that could not be told as any act, so it is not known what
   it would do.
3. intent is on the Never list and a law beside it applies on the day: escalate; when jurisdictions are given,
   only if such a law is one of theirs.
4. intent is on no list (a name these rules do not have): escalate.
5. intent is on the Closed list: escalate.
6. Otherwise: finish.

Triggers (6), each one passed when it happened at any point in the conversation, whatever the intent:
- customer_asked: the customer asked for a person (a human, an agent, a representative, a supervisor, a manager), or said they do not want to deal with the AI, in any words, once.
- distressed: the customer said they are frightened, panicking, crying or cannot cope, or spoke of a medical emergency, of harming themselves, or of a danger to someone's life now.
- angry: the customer insulted or swore at the company, its staff or the AI, or said they are angry or furious.
- bereavement: the customer said that someone has died, or the conversation is about the account, the plan or the affairs of someone who has died.
- threat: the customer threatened harm to anyone or to property, or said someone is threatening or forcing them.
- legal_claim: the customer spoke of a lawyer, a lawsuit, a court, a regulator or an ombudsman, a formal complaint or a formal appeal, or of taking legal action.

Never (25): account.refuse, claim.deny_medical, claim.refuse, collections.refuse, coverage.deny_medical, coverage.refuse, credit.refuse, decision.appeal, decision.review, dispute.refuse, fraud.refuse, insclaim.decide, insclaim.partial, insclaim.refuse, liability.decide, limit.lower, payment_arrangement.refuse, policy.cancel, policy.nonrenew, policy.refuse, priorauth.deny_medical, priorauth.refuse, refund.refuse, totalloss.decide, transfer.error_refuse

Weiser, No. 1:26-cv-01515 (D. Stat. § 58-50-61(d) (North Carolina: a medical doctor licensed in North Carolina); 40 P.S. § 991.2152(c) (Pennsylvania Act 146 of 2022: a licensed physician); Tex. Ins. Acts ch. 395, § 4 (T.C.A. § 56-7-3603(b) as numbered there) (Tennessee: a licensed physician or same-specialty professional); RCW 48.43.830(3)(a) (Washington, as amended by E2SSB 5395, 2026 ch. 157: a licensed physician or health professional); Ark. Code § 23-99-1111(c)(1) (Arkansas Act 575 of 2023: a physician); D.C. Code § 31-3875.06(a)(1) (District of Columbia: a physician); N.D.C.C. § 26.1-36.12-03 (North Dakota: a licensed physician or pharmacist); Utah Code § 31A-22-650(3)(e) (Utah: an individual who has knowledge of the medical condition or disease of the enrollee, or consults with a specialist who has); Utah Code § 31A-22-650(6)(e) (Utah SB 319, 2026: an adverse preauthorization determination regarding clinical or medical necessity is made by an individual who has knowledge of the medical condition or disease of the enrollee, or consults with a specialist who has, exercises independent medical judgment, and does not rely solely on recommendations from any other source; from 2027-01-01); 18 Del. Jurisdictions. Each is given by its code: ISO 3166-1 for a country (US, GB), ISO 3166-2 for a part of one
(US-WA), EU for the European Union; UK is read as GB. A code takes in the laws of what it is part or member of,
and a country's code the laws of its parts (the lists below): US is the laws of the United States and of each
state; US-WA, of the United States and of Washington; DE, of the EU and of Germany; EU, of the EU. Where several
are given, each is applied and the strictest is followed.

Days. A law applies from the day written beside its jurisdiction below (00:00 UTC), and from the day it is cited
when none is written. Before that day it sends no intent to a person; the intent is answered as if that law were
not beside it.
